title: 5 Simple Ways To Eliminate Stress From Your Teaching Life
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin offers five concrete strategies for reducing teacher stress: the 'decide-first' method of consciously committing to calm before students arrive each day; saying no more often, not just to extra duties but to gossip, procrastination, and negativity; accepting decisions outside one's control rather than ruminating on them; abandoning efforts to verbally convince students to behave, which he calls the most burdensome and least effective strategy; and shifting full responsibility for independent work back onto students rather than micromanaging or reteaching. He frames unmanaged stress as damaging not just to teachers' wellbeing but to their patience, judgment, and classroom energy, which students can sense even without a word being said. Linsin closes by acknowledging the strategies require real discipline and commitment, but insists that meaningful change begins with a single daily decision.
points: The 'decide-first' method — consciously committing to stay calm before students arrive, every day — is described as simple but genuinely transformative over time.
Teachers should say no more often, not only to extra responsibilities but to gossip, procrastination, and negative colleagues.
Accepting decisions outside one's control (new policies, curriculum mandates) quickly, rather than ruminating, reduces unnecessary stress.
Trying to verbally convince students to behave — counseling, scolding, persuading — is the most burdensome and least effective classroom management strategy.
Shifting full responsibility for independent work onto students, rather than micromanaging or re-teaching, reduces stress and prevents learned helplessness.
quotes: Stress is a killer. And not just physically. It can also ruin your teaching career.
The way it works is just before your students arrive for the day, shut your classroom door and allow yourself a few minutes of uninterrupted silence.
Nearly every teacher would benefit by using more of this two-letter word. If fact, if you don’t say no regularly, chances are that you’re overworked and near the end of your rope.

Besides being ineffective, trying to counsel, question, scold, guilt, coax, manipulate, persuade, or otherwise find the perfect words to get students to behave is incredibly burdensome and the most stressful strategy you can use.
Micromanaging, coddling, and over-helping very effectively produces learned helplessness. It dissuades listening and encourages dependence on you.
It also brings tense, negative energy into your classroom that you can't feel, but that visitors experience the moment they walk through your door.
